Macrons

Consonantal i

Consonantal u

Theme

Money, work & business · Town, shops & places

retail noun and adjective and verb

also retailer, retailers, sell retail, retail trade, retail shop, small trader

classical

Suet. Vesp. 16: coemendō quaedam tantum ut plūris posteā distraheret (Lewis & Short)
M-O s.v. sale: retail (mercēs distrahere)

distrahō, distrahere, distrāxī, distractum

verb, third conjugation, transitive

sell piecemeal, retail

In the language of trade, to sell off in separate lots (Lewis & Short, mostly post-Augustan); its first sense is to pull apart. Buying up in bulk is coemere.

Other words

  • propōla, propōlae m. — a retailer, a small dealer

    noun, first declension · also used · classical · Cic. Pis. 67: pānis et vīnum ā propōlā atque dē cūpā (Lewis & Short); Traupman 169: retailer

    Greek προπώλης: the dealer who sells to the public, often with a hint of the huckster. In Cicero’s line Piso’s bread and wine come from the shop and the cask, not from his own stores.

  • dīvēndō, dīvēndere, —, dīvēnditum — sell off in lots

    verb, third conjugation · also used · classical · Cic. Agr. 1.3 (Lewis & Short); Liv. 1.53 (Lewis & Short): praedam

    Rare (Lewis & Short): of property or booty sold off in parcels rather than of shop trade.

Examples

  • Hic propōla omnia cārius vēndit.

    This retailer sells everything at a higher price.composed

See also sell, seller, shop, shopkeeper, price.

SourcesLewis & Short: distraho · Lewis & Short: propola · Lewis & Short: divendo · Lewis & Short: coemo

Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. sale.

Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.

The example sentence marked “composed” is ours.
